aw_spirit_follower:
Spirit follower companion in Angkor Wat (~97 lines).

Spirit entity that follows the player through the temple.
Floats behind Will and provides ambient company during
the dungeon exploration. Uses smooth follow mechanics
to track player movement.
awB0_shrubber:
Shrubber enemy — plant creature in Angkor Wat (~118 lines).

Camouflaged enemy that hides in vegetation and attacks
when the player walks nearby. Surprise attack pattern
with brief visibility before striking.
awB0_zip_fly:
Zip Fly enemy — fast darting insect in Angkor Wat (~337 lines).

Extremely fast flying enemy with erratic flight patterns.
Darts at the player in quick bursts, pauses briefly, then
darts again. Difficult to hit due to speed. Complex
directional AI with random movement variation.
awB0_zombie:
Zombie enemy — undead with resurrection in Angkor Wat (~684 lines).

Complex undead enemy that rises from the ground when the
player approaches. Can resurrect after being defeated
unless destroyed quickly enough. Multi-phase AI with
shambling patrol, lunge attack, and death/resurrection
mechanics. One of the largest regular enemy scripts.
awB1_goldcap:
Goldcap enemy — mushroom creature in Angkor Wat (~200 lines).

Mushroom-type enemy with a defensive golden cap that
blocks attacks from above. Must be hit from the sides.
Releases spore projectiles when damaged. Uses directional
defense checks in hit callbacks.
awB1_gorgon:
Gorgon enemy — petrification creature in Angkor Wat (~397 lines).

The source of the stone girl curse in the Native Village.
Can petrify the player briefly on eye contact. Uses
directional facing checks to determine when the petrify
gaze connects. Multi-phase with standard melee and the
special gaze attack. Defeating all Gorgons lifts the curse.
awB1_wall_walker:
Wall Walker enemy — wall-traversing creature in Angkor Wat (~543 lines).

Unique enemy that walks along walls and ceilings, ignoring
normal collision. Drops down from above to attack. Complex
pathfinding that follows wall surfaces. When killed, can
trigger field reveals via deathActionIdx. Large script
with wall-following navigation logic.
debug_man:
Debug Man - an unused developer NPC that maxes the player's stats and offers a warp menu with 21 destinations (Bank 0B, 781856-782712). No scene script, scene_actors record or spawn call in extracted/ references it, so it never appears in the retail game.

=== STRUCTURE ===

The actor-def (sprite index 2, flags 0, header byte $10) entry runs once: MarkSolidHere, SetInteractHandler(DebugManInteract), SetEntryHere, RTL. Nothing runs per frame afterwards; talking to the NPC starts DebugManInteract.
DebugManInteract writes max HP and HP = 40, STR and DEF = 127 (16-bit stores, so the high bytes become 0) and abilityBitmask = $FF (all abilities), prints the greeting and opens the first menu. It does this on every conversation, so talking to Debug Man again resets the stats to those values.

=== MENU CHAIN ===

The menu is 7 levels. Each level is PrintDialogString (one page of 4 rows) followed by COP DialogueOptions( #04, #00, table ): the two operand bytes form the menu-layout word handed to MenuSelectionHandler, which returns 0 for B (cancel) or the confirmed row + 1. DialogueOptions uses that as the index into the word table and resumes the script there. Every table therefore has 5 entries: [0] = DebugManQuit (B), [1] to [4] = rows 1 to 4.
Row 1 of levels 1 to 6 is 'Others' and opens the next level; rows 2 to 4 are destinations. Level 7 has 'Quit' as row 1 (table entries 0 and 1 are both DebugManQuit) and three destinations.
A destination leaf prints 'Ok! See you again!', queues the scene change with COP QueueMapChange( scene, X px, Y px, facing, scroll params ) and returns with RTL. The facing byte is an index into direction_velocity_table (it selects the first sprite frame of the spawned player). The leaves change no stats and no flags.

=== DESTINATIONS (scene id, then the leaf label) ===

Level 1: Great Wall $82 (DebugWarpGreatWall), LAST GAIA LOOK = the ending sequence $E5 (DebugWarpLastGaiaLook), EDOWA-DO = Edward Castle $0A (DebugWarpEdowaDo). The ROM order of the last two leaves is the reverse of the row order; the table maps row 3 to the $E5 leaf and row 4 to the $0A leaf.
Level 2: Itory Village $15, Moon Tribe camp $1A, underground castle $0F. Level 3: Euro $91, Natives' Village $AC, Dao $C3. Level 4: Inca Ruins $1C, Freejia $32 (HANANOMIYAKO), Diamond Mine $3E (DAIYAMONDO).
Level 5: Sky Garden $4C, Seaside Palace $5A, Mu $5F. Level 6: Angel Village $69, a second entry point of Natives' Village $AC and of Dao $C3. Level 7: Pyramid $CC, Watermia $78, Angkor Wat $B0.
That is 21 leaves; the old header said about 35 destinations, and the old labels for $32 (Gold Ship) and $3E (Diamond Coast) and the swapped $0A / $E5 comments were wrong.
debug_stat_setter:
Unused debug actor (Bank 0B, 784986-785010): sets four player stats to $0040 and kills itself. Nothing in extracted/ spawns it - it is in no scene_actors list and no script spawn - so it is dead code kept in the ROM.

The four writes are playerStr, playerDef, playerMaxHp and hpToHeal, all $0040 (64). It does not touch playerHp, so the player's current HP only rises through the heal request. For comparison debug_man sets HP 40 / STR 127 / DEF 127 (plus the ability mask and a warp menu) and unused_debug_mode sets HP 19 / STR 32 / DEF 33.

The WRAM map describes hpToHeal as a heal request that the HUD plays out as the HP recovery animation; no reader of $0B22 was found in extracted/, so that is documentation only (see the questions file).
dialog_string_scanner:
Development tool: walks the ROM for COP PrintDialogString calls and shows each dialog string (Bank 0B, 778693-778807). No scene, script or table references it (an unscened actor).

HOW IT FINDS STRINGS: the word $BF02 is the byte pair 02 BF, a COP instruction with signature $BF = PrintDialogString (copdef), followed by its 2-byte operand, a pointer to the string in the script's own bank (&DialogString). The scanner compares a word at every offset, reads the operand after a hit and shows the string through DialogStringRenderer with DBR = the scanned bank, so the pointer resolves in the right bank. The old header called $BF02 a 'dialog string header marker'.

POINTER TEST: IsNotLoromAddress sets carry for values BELOW 0x8000 and clears it for 0x8000 and up, and the caller skips a hit on carry set (BCS). A string is therefore shown only when the operand is at least 0x8000 (a LoROM address). The old header and the inline notes had this reversed.

SCAN RANGE: the bank counter $24 is a 16-bit word that starts at $85 and is incremented per bank. The loop ends only when it equals $000C, which happens after the word wraps through $FFFF. Each pass takes the LOW byte as the bank (PHA / PLB), so banks $85-$FF come first, then banks $00-$FF again and again; the old 'banks $85 to $0B' (and the doc's '$85-$8C') do not match the code. Banks after the first are scanned from offset $0000, which on LoROM is not ROM for banks $80-$BF. In practice the halt loop is not reached.

SAVED STATE: $0100 = the scan offset after a hit, $0102 = a 16-bit copy of the stack top (the bank byte plus the low byte of the pointer). Only system_core's startup check reads $0100 (a leftover resume test).

START: runs only while worldReadyFlag ($0654) is nonzero and positive (negative = loading); until then it returns every frame.
diary_entry_table:
Diary location table (Bank 0B, 256 pointers = 512 bytes, then 23 diary-entry records). Index = scene ID; the diary menu looks up the scene saved in each slot ($0D74 / $0D76 / $0D78, 0 = empty, filled by DiaryScanSramSlots) to print the location name and to pan the Mode 7 camera.

Each diary-entry is a name string closed by $CA (not shown) followed by 4 bytes printed in memory order: the camera target X word and the camera target Y word (little-endian). DiaryCameraPan scans for the $CA, reads the two words and moves cameraTargetX / cameraTargetY towards them. The default entry's (X, Y) = ($0080, $0300) is the diary menu's initial camera. The [ADR:&diary_entry_table,D74] tokens of the slot strings print the name by the same lookup.

The table is the 256-word jump table; 221 scenes point at the default entry ('Start from beginning') and 35 scenes (the places that have a Dark Space and a save) at 22 named locations. Names with a trailing space ('Itory Village ', 'City of Euro ', 'Natives' Village ') are in the ROM that way.

=== CORRECTIONS ===

The old header said the 4 bytes are a 'packed camera position value'. They are two words (X, Y), not packed. docs/structs-reference.md calls diary-entry a 'warp destination' with 'scene ID + X/Y coordinates'; the entry holds no scene ID (the scene is the table index) and nothing warps with it: the load goes to scene $E6 (DiaryStartLoadConfirm).
dm_mine_static_prop: Static decorative prop in the Diamond Mine inner area. Non-interactive scene element.
gs_gold_ship_intro_text: Gold Ship intro text dialog string. Story text displayed when first exploring the Incan Gold Ship.
gw82_archer:
Archer enemy — ranged attacker on the Great Wall (~719 lines).

Fires arrows at the player from fixed positions. Complex AI
with firing angle calculations based on player position.
Multiple arrow types with different speeds and trajectories.
Patrols along wall sections and shoots when player enters
range. Includes arrow child actors for the projectiles.
gw82_eyesore:
Eyesore enemy — floating eye creature on the Great Wall.

Flying enemy that tracks the player and fires projectile
attacks. Uses BranchOnPlayer* for directional aiming.
Moves erratically with aerial movement patterns, making
it difficult to hit consistently.
gw82_fire_bug:
Fire Bug enemy — flame-carrying insect on the Great Wall.

Fast-moving enemy with contact fire damage. Moves in erratic
patterns with directional sprite animation. Burns the player
on contact. Common enemy in the wall corridor sections.
gw82_wall_spear:
Wall spear trap — retractable spear hazard on the Great Wall.

Environmental trap that extends from the wall at timed
intervals. Damages the player on contact during extension.
Timer-based cycle. Common corridor hazard throughout
the Great Wall dungeon.
gw83_asp:
Asp enemy — snake enemy on the Great Wall (~573 lines).

Ground-based serpent with fast strike attacks. Coils and
lunges toward the player. Complex multi-phase AI with
patrol, alert, and attack states. Uses directional movement
with solid collision checks. Found in the wall's inner rooms.
gw88_short_wall_spear:
Short wall spear trap in the Great Wall tomb area.

Variant of wall_spear with modified timing for the tomb
rooms. Shorter extension period creating quick-fire hazards
in the narrow tomb corridors.
gw8A_sand_fanger:
Sand Fanger boss fight — Great Wall area boss (~1,610 lines).

The largest boss script in the game. Multi-phase sand worm
boss that burrows underground and surfaces to attack.
Uses position prediction to emerge near the player. Multiple
attack types: sand spray, lunging bite, tail sweep. Phase
transitions increase speed and attack variety. The arena
has shifting sand terrain. Defeat triggers Mystic Statue
reward: "You've defeated the Sand Fanger! Look! A Mystic Statue!"
mtA0_acid_spider:
Acid Spider — major enemy in the Mountain Temple (~735 lines).

Large spider enemy with acid spit ranged attacks. Patrols
temple corridors and clings to walls. Complex multi-phase
AI with web mechanics, ceiling traversal, and acid
projectile patterns. One of the game's largest regular
enemy scripts.
mtA0_skulker:
Skulker enemy in the Mountain Temple (~228 lines).

Stealthy enemy that hides in dark areas and ambushes the
player. Uses visibility detection based on player distance.
Lunges from hiding with a quick melee attack, then retreats
to a new hiding position.
mtA1_fire_sprite:
Fire Sprite enemy in the Mountain Temple (~429 lines).

Floating flame enemy with complex orbital movement patterns.
Circles around fixed points and fires projectile attacks
at the player. Uses math_lookup_tables for sine/cosine
movement. Leaves fire trail hazards.
mtA1_yorrick_ew:
Yorrick enemy (east-west variant) in the Mountain Temple (~201 lines).

Skull enemy that patrols east-west corridors. Bounces
off walls and reverses direction. Damages on contact.
The east-west variant has horizontal movement priority.
mtA1_yorrick_ns:
Yorrick enemy (north-south variant) in the Mountain Temple (~192 lines).

Skull enemy that patrols north-south corridors. Same
mechanics as the east-west variant but with vertical
movement priority. Used in vertical passages.
mummy_queen_angle_table:
Angle lookup data table for the Mummy Queen's orbital attacks.

Small data table (10 lines) containing pre-computed angles
used by the queen's orb projectiles for their circular
movement patterns.
pr_text_placement_calc:
Prologue text placement calculator (~138 lines).

Computes screen positions for the prologue's scrolling
and fading text display. Handles centering, line spacing,
character-by-character reveal timing, and fade effects
for the opening narrative.
pr_thinkers: Prologue thinker sprites. Animated character sprites used during the prologue historical narrative sequences.
pr8C_prologue1:
Prologue 1: the prophecy (~137 lines).

Opening narrative establishing the ancient prophecy about
the comet's cyclical return. Animated text sequences with
the game's first visual storytelling. Sets the mythological
foundation for the entire plot.
pr8C_prologue5:
Prologue 5: return to the prophecy (~115 lines).

Concluding prologue segment that loops back to the prophecy
theme and transitions into the game's opening at South Cape.
Bridges the mythological backstory to Will's personal story.
pr8D_prologue2:
Prologue 2: the legends (~237 lines).

Second prologue segment. Continues the opening narrative
with animated text and character silhouettes showing the
legends of past civilizations affected by the comet's
cyclical return. Extensive scripted text sequences.
pr8E_prologue3:
Prologue 3: the missing (~124 lines).

Third prologue segment about Will's father's disappearance
at the Tower of Babel. Establishes Will's motivation to
search for his father. Transitions to the game's opening.
pr8F_prologue4:
Prologue 4: the mishap.

Brief narrative (~38 lines) about the Tower of Babel
expedition's tragic outcome. Will's father Olman and
the exploration party vanished during the expedition.
pyCC_blaster:
Blaster enemy — ranged Pyramid defender.

Stationary enemy that fires projectiles at the player
when in range. Uses directional aiming with BranchOnPlayer*
to target shots. Standard Pyramid corridor enemy.
pyCC_mystic_ball:
Mystic Ball enemy — floating magical sphere in the Pyramid.

Hovering enemy (~257 lines) that orbits through rooms and
fires energy projectiles. When defeated, can trigger a
field reveal effect if deathActionIdx is set. Uses movement
patterns with direction switching on wall collision.
pyCE_tuts:
Tuts enemy — mummy warrior in the Pyramid (~282 lines).

Melee enemy that patrols corridors and charges at the player.
Uses 4-directional movement with animated wrapping attacks.
Moderately armored with pursuit AI based on player proximity.
pyD2_haunt:
Haunt enemy — ghost in the Pyramid (~294 lines).

Phase-shifting ghost that alternates between solid and
translucent states. Can only be damaged while solid.
Teleports to random positions near the player and fires
projectiles during the solid phase. Complex AI with
timing-based vulnerability windows.
pyDD_mummy_queen:
Mummy Queen boss fight — Pyramid area boss (~627 lines).

Multi-phase boss with orbital energy orb attacks, spirit
summons, teleportation across the arena, and invulnerability
phases. Uses multiple child actors: queen_orb_shot for
projectile orbs, queen_spirit_attack for spirit summons,
queen_debris for environmental hazards, and queen_phase_transition
for phase shift animations. Arena boundaries managed by
queen_arena_boundary. Defeat grants the Mystic Statue.
pyDD_queen_arena_boundary:
Mummy Queen arena boundary walls — invisible collision.

Defines the boss arena's playable area by creating
invisible collision barriers. Prevents the player from
leaving the fight zone during the battle.
pyDD_queen_debris:
Mummy Queen debris hazard — falling rubble during the fight.

Environmental hazard spawned during boss phase transitions.
Debris falls from above and damages the player on contact.
Creates visual chaos and movement pressure.
pyDD_queen_invincible_orb:
Mummy Queen invincible orb — shields the boss.

Small child actor (16 lines) that orbits the queen during
invulnerability phases. Cannot be destroyed. Blocks player
attacks and deals contact damage.
pyDD_queen_orb_shot:
Mummy Queen orb projectile — homing energy attack (~151 lines).

Projectile child spawned by the queen. Launches from the
boss position and tracks toward the player using movement
prediction. Can be blocked by Shadow form's special ability.
Multiple orbs spawn simultaneously during attack phases.
pyDD_queen_phase_transition:
Mummy Queen phase transition animation controller (~101 lines).

Manages the visual effects and timing between boss phases.
Handles the queen's teleportation, invulnerability flash,
and arena environment changes between phases.
pyDD_queen_spirit_attack:
Mummy Queen spirit summon attack (~109 lines).

Spirit projectile that emerges from the queen and flies
toward the player. Passes through walls. Used in the
queen's later phases as a harder-to-dodge attack type.
pyDD_teleporter:
Teleporter pads in the Mummy Queen lair (~204 lines).

Interactive warp points that move the player between
different positions in the boss arena. The queen also
uses these to reposition during the fight. Manages
both player-initiated and script-triggered teleportation.
s89_new_babel:
New Babel overview — the transformed world.

Brief scene: "The Earth's look had changed, but, glowing in
the sky, it was as beautiful as ever. Buildings and cities..."
Shows the post-comet world with rebuilt civilization.
s90_changed_world:
Changed world overview — continents have shifted.

Story scene (~76 lines). Will: "Somehow the land has taken on
a strange shape." Will's father: "That's the new world."
Kara observes the transformed globe. Visual scene showing
the continents rearranging into their modern positions
after the comet's influence.
sE5_epilogue:
Epilogue cutscene after Dark Gaia's defeat (~261 lines).

The story conclusion. Kara: "What's happened to the comet...?"
Will's father: "The comet's power has disappeared. The evil
star has flown off to the other side..." Extended dialog
between Will, Kara, and Olman wrapping up the plot.
Transitions to the credits sequence.
sFA_diary_menu:
Diary / save menu actor for scene $FA (Bank 0B, 778810-783347 plus the dialog strings): the 4-tab menu shown after the title screen - Start Journey, Erase Trip Diary, Copy Trip Diary, Change Snd/Buttons - over the three save slots.

Entry: TitleToDiaryTransition (sFC_title_start_handler) queues scene $FA at ($100,$370); the prologue scenes $8C-$8F also spawn the Start-poll actor sFC_title_start_poll, so Start there lands here too. The scene background is the overworld map (scene_meta_00FA: display-mode #08, set_overworld / map_overworld_main, music bgm_beautiful_world). DiaryCameraPan scrolls it to the location stored in diary_entry_table for the highlighted slot's source scene.

=== DISPLAY SETUP (DiaryMenuInit) ===

TM = $01 (BG1), TS = $04 (BG3 on the sub screen), so the BG3 text is colour-math-blended over BG1: CGWSEL = $82 (main screen forced black inside the colour window, addend = sub screen), CGADSUB = $41 (add, half intensity, BG1 only). WOBJSEL = $22 enables window 1 for the colour window and the OBJ window; WH0/WH1 are fed by diary_menu_window_dma, which draws the highlight bands (see that file). W34SEL = $88 enables window 2 for BG3/BG4. The camera starts at ($80,$300); displayModeFlags |= $4001 (bit 14 = HUD off, bit 0 = full BG3 upload). Start and Select are masked out of joypadCurrent ($3000 in joypadMaskStd), playerFlags $2800 (script lock $0800 + guard stance $2000) is set until the menu leaves, and the D-pad auto-repeats ($0F00 in joypadMaskInv). The black-inside-window look is decoded from the registers, not observed (OQ-I057-3).
RunBg3Script consolestring_01EADC draws the button legend box (A Button: Enter / B Button: Cancel).

=== DIARY STATE BLOCK ($0D74-$0D9E) ===

| Address | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| $0D74/76/78 | Source scene ID (sourceSceneId $0B12 of the slot's save page) for slots 1/2/3; 0 = empty or invalid |
| $0D7A/7C/7E | Max HP (playerMaxHp $0ACA) for slots 1/2/3 |
| $0D80/82/84 | DEF (playerDef $0ADC) for slots 1/2/3 |
| $0D86/88/8A | STR (playerStr $0ADE) for slots 1/2/3 |
| $0D8C | Active / last-used slot (0-2), mirrored in SRAM $306000 |
| $0D8E | Button type setting (0 = Type 1, 1 = Type 2); saved in the slot page at $0B26 |
| $0D90 | Sound setting (0 = stereo, 1 = mono); saved in the slot page at $0B24 |
| $0D92 | Slot cursor (0-2, $FFFF = none); drives the slot band |
| $0D94 | Slot being edited (Snd/Buttons editor, arrangement screen, erase prompt) |
| $0D96 | Copy target slot ($FFFF = none); drives a second slot band |
| $0D98 | Tab cursor (0-3) or settings-row cursor (0-2), $FFFF = none; drives the narrow band |
| $0D9A/9C/9E | BCD scratch for the stat strings: HP / STR / DEF |

=== SRAM LAYOUT ===

$306000 holds the last-used slot (0-2). Slot n's page is $306200 + n*512: a copy of WRAM $0A00-$0BFB (508 bytes). Its additive checksum is at $3063FC + n*512 and its XOR checksum at $3063FE + n*512 (both seeded with $3652, computed by save_system.ComputeSaveChecksum with X = n*512). The two settings live inside the page at $0B24 (sound) and $0B26 (button type).

=== BUTTON TYPES ===

ApplySoundAndRemap (run when a game starts) reads sound $0B24 and button type $0B26. Type 1 (0) sets remapA = $8000, remapB = $4000, remapX = 0, remapY = $0040; Type 2 (1) only sets remapX = 0 and leaves the other remaps at their current values (the engine defaults). The on-screen legend (dialogstring_0BF63F / 0BF653) reads 'Type 1: A, B, SEL, Y' and 'Type 2: B, Y, SEL, A' against the rows Attack/Talk, Item/Cancel, Item palette, Not used. This baserom's system_init transform changes the default remaps (remapA $8080, remapB $4008, remapY $0040, remapX $0004) and the menu's own button tests ($8000 confirm, $4000 cancel), so what Type 2 does here is unverified (OQ-I057-1).
The erase prompt temporarily remaps B/Y in vanilla; transforms.json strips those stubs from the plain extraction, but multi-line rules do not apply under extract:lt (OQ-I026-1), so the stubs stay visible in the line-tracked text.

=== UNREFERENCED CODE ===

Nine routines carry the _noref suffix and have no callers: a BG3 cursor engine (DiaryCursorNav_noref; its helpers DiaryCursorApplyMove ... DiaryClearAllCursors and diary_cursor_menu_table are only reached from it), a controller-2 debug set at 782712-783013 (DiaryJoypadFilter_noref, DiaryResetCounter_noref, DiaryIncCounter_noref, DiaryDigitDisplay_noref, DiaryUnused24B_noref, DiaryReadJoy2_noref, DiaryNullHandler_noref, DiaryAwaitButtonRelease_noref). DiaryMenuVBlankHandler is a copy of VBlankWaitAndJoypad whose only caller is the unreferenced DiaryAwaitButtonRelease_noref; the live menu uses the engine's VBlankWaitAndJoypad and its remap.
sFB_boot_logo:
Boot logo sequence actor - scene $FB master controller (the first scene of the game). Scene $FB is entered TWICE at power-on and shows one logo per visit; the second logo then hands over to the title screen scene $FC.

=== SEQUENCE ===

1. BootLogoInit (both visits): sets displayModeFlags bit 14 (no reader found, OQ-I034-1), clears colour 0 of the palette staging buffer, enables FastROM (MEMSEL = $01), puts only the sprite layer on the main screen (TM = $10, bit 4 = OBJ; no BG is shown), masks the joypad, then reads STAT78 bit 4: 0 = 60 Hz NTSC continues, 1 = 50 Hz PAL jumps to BootLogoPalLockout.
2. First visit (event flag $10 clear): nudge the actor Y -16, play sprite animation #01 (sprite_group_000112, a 96 x 48 logo on OBJ palette 3) for 2 passes of 60 ticks = 120 ticks, set event flag $10, QueueMapChange to scene $FB itself, Die.
3. Second visit (flag set): BootLogoSecondPhase plays animation #00 (sprite_group_000010, the Enix logo: an emblem with a wordmark under it, OBJ palettes 0, 1, 2 and 4) for 120 ticks, clears flag $10 and queues scene $FC (title screen), Die.
Event flag $10 is not one of the flags the scene load zeroes (only $00 to $0F are), which is why it survives the reload; it is cleared again at the end because the South Cape church scripts (sc08_*) use the same flag.

The three boot_logo_enix_palette_obj* thinkers are spawned by the scene's thinker list in both visits and run the Enix logo's palette cycle on OBJ palettes 0, 1 and 2, i.e. only the second logo (see boot_logo_enix_palette_obj0).

=== PAL LOCKOUT ===

A 50 Hz console never sees a logo: BootLogoPalLockout draws the region warning text (consolestring_01D9D8) on BG3 and then yields forever at SetEntryHere + RTL. The game cannot be started on a PAL console.

=== POSITION ===

The scene's actor-spawn places the actor at tile (7, 8) and InitActorFromSceneData adds 8 pixels of X for normal actors; the first NudgePosition adds another 8, so the actor ends at X = 128, the centre of the 256-pixel screen. The sprite groups are laid out around that origin. QueueMapChange's last operand $1100 is the packed camera-bounds override (InitCameraBounds).

=== SPRITES (spm_boot_logos.sprite.asm) ===

The scene's spritemap card loads spm_boot_logos ($018F bytes) to $7E4000; its two entries are the animation indexes of StageSpriteLoop: #00 = sprite_set_000004 (second logo), #01 = sprite_set_00000A (first logo). Each sprite-set is one frame record (hold $003B = 60 ticks per pass, group pointer) closed by the hidden $FFFF delimiter.
First logo, sprite_group_000112: 96 x 48 px, 16 parts of 16 x 16 in rows of 6, 6 and 4, all OBJ palette 3.
Second logo, sprite_group_000010: 122 x 156 px, 35 parts: a 4 x 4 block (64 x 64) on OBJ palette 1 (upper two rows) and 0 (lower two rows), a 4 x 2 block below it on palette 2, and a row of 11 parts 12 px apart on palette 4. Palettes 0 to 2 are the ones the boot_logo_enix_palette_obj* thinkers animate; palette 4 is static.
Sprite-part = 7 bytes: size flag, X offset and mirrored X, Y offset and mirrored Y, OAM tile word (high byte vhppPPPN, PPP = OBJ palette). Sprite-group = 12 header bytes (X extents left / right, Y extents above / below, 8 bytes nothing reads, identical in both groups), the part count, then the parts. The palettes come from pal_boot_logos (80 colours, OBJ palettes 0 to 4, loaded at CGRAM colour 128). The second logo is the Enix logo (its palette cycle is the three boot_logo_enix_palette_obj* thinkers); which company the first logo belongs to was not checked against the tile art.

=== NOTES ===

The joypad mask in the ROM is $FFFC (db-us/transforms.json rewrites $FFF0 to $FFFC for this block), which hides every pad bit including Start and Select, so no logo can be skipped. The old header said TM = $10 puts BG1 on the main screen and that the mask is $FFF0; TM bit 4 is the OBJ layer and the shipped mask is $FFFC.
sFC_title_intro:
Title scene $FC intro actor (Bank 0B, 772391-772487, plus the comet actor and an unreferenced palette-fade stub below it). Spawned with sFC_title_start_handler by scene_event_0CE56D, the title scene's actor list.

Loads the title palette, spawns TitleCometSpriteActor, shows two BG3 text strings on a timer and, after a ~42-second idle period (WaitWord $09D3 = 2516 ticks), sets event flag $F4 and queues scene $8C (the prologue). Flag $F4 is tested by pr8C_prologue1 (BranchOnFlagByte, branch when clear) and pr8C_prologue5 (branch when set) and cleared again in pr8C_prologue1, so it marks 'the prologue was started by the title's idle timeout'.

=== DISPLAY LAYERS ===

TM starts at $10 (OBJ only: the comet sprites are the first thing on screen; the title picture is not on a main-screen layer yet). TitleCometSpriteActor later writes TM = $16 (BG2 + BG3 + OBJ) after its sprite animation, which brings in the title picture and the BG3 text layer.

=== TEXT TIMING ===

Two BG3 text scripts are shown in sequence:
- consolestring_01DA5E after WaitByte $B3 (180 ticks, ~3 seconds)
- consolestring_01DA47 after WaitByte $77 more (120 ticks, ~2 seconds)
sFC_title_start_handler:
Title / prologue Start handler (Bank 0B, 772529-772609): waits for Start, then sends the game to the diary menu (scene $FA).

Two actor-defs share one poll loop. sFC_title_start_handler is spawned with sFC_title_intro by scene_event_0CE56D (the title scene $FC list) and first waits WaitWord $021B = 540 ticks (~9 s) so the intro's opening seconds cannot be skipped. sFC_title_start_poll polls at once; it is spawned in the actor lists of the four prologue scenes ($8C-$8F, next to pr8C_prologue1/5, pr8D_prologue2, pr8E_prologue3 and pr8F_prologue4), so Start skips the prologue slides as well.

Both variants first mask nearly every button out of joypadCurrent (joypadMaskStd |= $FFFC; vanilla $FFF0, widened by transforms.json) and then poll with COP BranchIfPressed #$1001. In that mask word bit 0 is not a button: it makes the handler test joypadRaw instead of joypadCurrent (see docs/cop/families/input.md, BranchIfPressed), which is how Start ($1000) still gets through the mask. R is not tested.

On Start, TitleToDiaryTransition sets transitionBrightness = 0 and the transition parameters (gfxCacheIdxB = 0: speed 0; gfxCacheIdxA = 1: exit type 1 = instant blank, enter type 0 = graduated fade), queues scene $FA at ($0100,$0370) with COP QueueMapChange, yields one frame, runs one VBlankWaitAndJoypad with DP forced to $0000, and then holds INIDISP = $00 (force blank) every frame until the scene change replaces the actor.
unused_particle_rain_spawner:
Particle rain spawner (Bank 0B, 774827-774918): a looping actor that spawns falling particle children at an increasing rate, plus the child (UnusedRainDropChild). It is NOT used: no spawn table, script or thinker references unused_particle_rain_spawner anywhere in extracted/ (the old header said 'used for the ending credits particle rain'; docs/code/bank0B... lists it as unreferenced). actor-def <#00,#00,#38>.

=== SPAWNER ===

$24 starts at $78. Each cycle: if $24 is not 4, decrement it; store $24 in the wait counter $08; SetEntryHereAndYield; spawn a child. The wait counter resumes the actor after N + 1 ticks (see WaitByte), so the intervals are 120, 119, 118 ... 5 ticks and then 5 ticks forever (the old note said the delay shrinks to 4 frames; the real minimum is 5). The spawn rate therefore RISES with time: the old part note called this 'decelerating'; only the delay decelerates. The ramp takes 7,250 ticks (about 2 minutes) to reach the steady rate. UNVERIFIED-RUNTIME.
COP SpawnAfterFlags ( @UnusedRainDropChild, #$1802 ) writes $1802 into the child's flags word $10; CopyActorState copies the spawner's position, anim index and pointers.

=== CHILD ===

SetMetasprite points the child at spriteset_enemies and StageSprAndHitbox #02 shows animation list 2 (sprite_set_0EE0A6: 7 frames, hold 2 each, so one pass is 21 ticks). Priority operand $30 sets OAM priority bits $3000 (frontmost). Start: Y = $FFE0 (-32), X = RNG * 2 + $C4, i.e. $C4-$2C2 in steps of 2. The same random byte also picks the speed: index = (RNG AND 3) * 2 + 4.
The values stored in moveXAlt / moveYAlt are MOVEMENT INDICES into movement_delta_table, not velocities (the old comments said 'X velocity 4, 6, 8, 10 / Y velocity 3, 5, 7, 9'). Odd indices are +n, even indices are -n pixels per frame (index 3 = +2, 4 = -2, 5 = +3, 6 = -3 ...). The child therefore moves X by -2, -3, -4 or -5 and Y by +2, +3, +4 or +5 per frame (index X = 4/6/8/10 pairs with Y = 3/5/7/9, equal magnitudes): it falls DIAGONALLY down and to the left at 45 degrees, not straight down.
ReloadMoveDurations re-arms the two delta chains; AnimOnce zeroes $2C / $2E when its list ends, which is why the loop reloads them after every pass. The death test (Y >= $0200, unsigned) runs only when an animation pass has ended, i.e. every 21 ticks, not every frame. A particle whose Y were still negative at that moment would be read as a huge unsigned value and die; at 21 ticks the slowest particle (+2 per frame from -32) is at +10, so by the numbers all of them survive the first check (UNVERIFIED-RUNTIME, OQ-I045-2).

docs/code/bank0B-late-bosses-system-cutscene-actors.md also says the particles 'rise via ReloadForceMove' from 'screen top'; they start above the screen and FALL.
